name: Metadata Filtering
question: Can I search by meaning and still respect hard facts?
summary: Combine vector similarity with structured conditions on each chunk, such as date, product, region, document type or version, so the top k are the nearest chunks that also match. Where the filter runs matters: after the vector search (post-filtering), before it with an exact scan (pre-filtering), or inside the index walk with payload indexes (filtered ANN). Access control and multi-tenancy are a separate technique, and extracting filters from a user’s words belongs to agentic retrieval in RAG Pipelines.
useCases: Questions scoped to a product, region, date range or document version
Catalogues and knowledge bases where a rare filter must still return a full top k
Replacing “please only use 2025 circulars” in the prompt with a guaranteed condition

items.detail: share of chunks that match the filter; 0.5% means 10,000 of 20 lakh
ANN top k first, then drop non-matching; expected survivors = k × selectivity
find matching ids first, then score them exactly; cost grows with the matching count
the filter is checked during the graph walk (Qdrant, Weaviate ACORN, pgvector iterative scans)
a keyword, number or date index on a field; lets the planner estimate cardinality
fetch more candidates than k so enough survive a filter

steps: List the fields users filter on and store them as typed metadata at ingestion
Create payload or attribute indexes on those fields before the bulk load
Filter inside the vector query, not in application code after it
Measure recall@k and latency per selectivity band: broad, medium and rare filters
pitfalls: Post-filtering a top 10 with a rare filter returns few or no results
Pre-filtering a broad filter turns into a slow exact scan of most of the collection
Unindexed or inconsistent metadata (“MH” vs “Maharashtra”) silently drops matches
remember: Filter inside the search, index what you filter, test the rare filters.
caption: Illustrative: Suraksha General, a fictional insurer, with 20 lakh chunks. Expected survivors of a post-filter = 10 × selectivity.

comparison.needs: Queries scoped by date, product, region or version
comparison.best: Post-filter recall collapse on rare filters

code.text: C = "suraksha_docs"          # 2,000,000 chunks: wordings, circulars, claim notes
# 0.5% of the collection: the planner scans those exactly via the payload index
# the anti-pattern: top 10 first, filter afterwards
kept = [p for p in top if p.payload["region"] == "MH"]   # usually empty

steps.title: Index the fields you filter on
steps.text: Every field a query will filter on gets a payload index: keywords for product, region and document type, a datetime index for the effective date. Create them before the bulk upload, so the HNSW graph is built with the extra links that keep filtered walks connected.

steps.title: Store metadata with every chunk
steps.text: Each chunk carries its structured facts as payload: motor, Maharashtra, circular, version 3, effective from 1 April 2025. Metadata that is missing or free text at ingestion cannot be filtered on later.

steps.title: Write the filter as structure
steps.text: The filter is data, not words in the query: product = motor AND region = MH AND doc_type = circular AND effective_from ≥ 1 April 2025. Embedding “motor circulars for Maharashtra” only nudges similarity; a filter enforces it.

steps.title: Filter inside the search
steps.text: query_filter goes with the query vector, so the engine checks the condition while it walks the graph and only matching chunks enter the top 10. hnsw_ef widens the candidate list when the filter is strict.

steps.title: Let the planner use cardinality
steps.text: The filter matches about 10,000 of 20,00,000 chunks, or 0.5%. For a set that small, Qdrant's planner reads the matching ids from the payload index and scores them exactly: 10,000 distances, 100% recall, a few milliseconds.

steps.title: Never filter after a small top-k
steps.text: The anti-pattern searches first and filters afterwards. With 0.5% of chunks matching, the global top 10 holds 10 × 0.005 = 0.05 matching chunks on average, so the list usually comes back empty. Measure recall per selectivity band, not only on unfiltered queries.

pros: Answers respect hard facts: product, region, date and version
Filtering inside the search keeps a full, accurate top 10 even for rare filters
Payload indexes let the engine switch to an exact scan when the matching set is small
Fewer irrelevant chunks reach the prompt, so answers are shorter and cheaper
cons: Metadata must be clean and complete at ingestion time
Every filtered field needs an index, which costs memory and build time
Recall must be measured per selectivity band, not just overall
Very strict filters on engines without filter-aware indexes fall back to slow scans
avoidWhen: Queries rarely constrain structured fields (plain semantic search is enough)
The “filter” is fuzzy intent such as “recent-ish” or “about claims” (let ranking or a re-ranker handle it)

playgroundGuide.scenario: Suraksha General, a fictional insurer, has 20 lakh chunks of policy wordings, circulars and claim notes in one vector index. A claims handler wants the 10 nearest chunks that also match a structured filter: all motor documents (50% of chunks), motor documents for Maharashtra (5%), or motor circulars for Maharashtra since April 2025 (0.5%). You choose where the filter runs and how many candidates the search fetches.
controls: Choose the filter strategy: post-filter, pre-filter with an exact scan, or filtered ANN with a payload index.
Choose how selective the filter is: 50%, 5% or 0.5% of the chunks match.
Drag oversampling to fetch 10, 40, 200 or 1,000 candidates before the top 10 are chosen.

missions.text: With the 0.5% filter, return a full 10 results at 99% recall or better, in 10 ms or less.
missions.hint: Few chunks match, so scoring them exactly is cheap: pre-filter, or let filtered ANN hand the query to its planner.

missions.text: Show post-filtering returning fewer than 3 results even with at least 4× oversampling.
missions.hint: Use post-filtering with the 5% or 0.5% filter and 40 or 200 candidates.

missions.text: With the 50% filter, reach at least 95% recall with all 10 results in 10 ms or less.
missions.hint: Pre-filtering scans a million vectors here. Oversample a little, or filter inside the graph walk.

practice.scenario: Suraksha General, a fictional insurer, keeps 20 lakh chunks of policy wordings, IRDAI circulars and claim notes in Postgres with pgvector. A handler asks about motor own-damage rules for Maharashtra from April 2025. The query filters on product, region, document type and effective date inside the SQL, with a composite B-tree index on those columns and iterative HNSW scans switched on, so the top 10 are always ten matching chunks, even when only 0.5% of the table matches.

industries.use: Policy wordings and circulars filtered by product, state and effective date before an answer is drafted
“Running shoes like this, size 9, in stock in Bengaluru” as similarity plus size, stock and city filters
RBI master directions searched by meaning, restricted to the current version and a department

practice.analogy: A library catalogue search that first narrows to the right shelf, language and edition, then asks the librarian for the closest books on that shelf, instead of taking the ten closest books in the building and throwing away those on the wrong shelf.

library.name: pgvector
library.what: Postgres extension for vector search. Filters are ordinary WHERE clauses; since version 0.8.0, iterative index scans keep scanning the HNSW or IVFFlat index until enough rows pass the filter.
library.install: pip install "psycopg[binary]" pgvector  # plus CREATE EXTENSION vector; in Postgres

practice.note: The embed() function is a stub for your embedding model. hnsw.iterative_scan needs pgvector 0.8.0 or later. With relaxed_order, rows can come back slightly out of distance order; re-sort in an outer query if exact order matters. For very selective filters the Postgres planner may use the B-tree index and score the matching rows exactly, which is pre-filtering; check with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

samples.code:
import datetime as dt
import psycopg
from pgvector.psycopg import register_vector

conn = psycopg.connect("dbname=suraksha", autocommit=True)
register_vector(conn)

conn.execute("""
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS chunks_emb_hnsw
    ON chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS chunks_meta_idx
    ON chunks (product, region, doc_type, effective_from);
""")

def embed(text):
    """Stub: return a numpy float32 vector from your embedding model."""
    raise NotImplementedError

def search(question, product, region, doc_type, since, k=10):
    qvec = embed(question)
    with conn.transaction():
        conn.execute("SET LOCAL hnsw.ef_search = 100")
        conn.execute("SET LOCAL hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order")
        conn.execute("SET LOCAL hnsw.max_scan_tuples = 40000")
        return conn.execute("""
            SELECT id, title, embedding <=> %s AS distance
            FROM chunks
            WHERE product = %s AND region = %s
              AND doc_type = %s AND effective_from >= %s
            ORDER BY embedding <=> %s
            LIMIT %s""",
            (qvec, product, region, doc_type, since, qvec, k)).fetchall()

rows = search("own-damage claim rules after flooding", "motor", "MH",
              "circular", dt.date(2025, 4, 1))
for row in rows:
    print(row)

numericDrill.question: A search post-filters its ANN results by region. The region filter matches 2% of chunks, and filter values are spread evenly. How many candidates must the ANN search fetch so that, on average, 10 survive the filter?
numericDrill.answer: Expected survivors = candidates × selectivity, so candidates = 10 ÷ 0.02 = 500. Fetching the usual 10 would leave 0.2 on average. At 0.2% selectivity you would need 5,000, which is why rare filters belong inside the search.

interview.question: Pre-filtering, post-filtering or filtered ANN: how do you choose?
interview.answer: Look at selectivity. Post-filtering is only safe for broad filters and needs oversampling of about k ÷ selectivity. Pre-filtering with an exact scan is ideal when few items match, because scoring 10,000 vectors is cheap. Filtered ANN, where the index checks the filter during the graph walk, covers the middle and broad cases. Engines such as Qdrant choose between exact and graph search from the estimated cardinality, so index the filtered fields and test recall per band.

interview.question: Why can filtered HNSW lose recall, and how do engines fix it?
interview.answer: A strict filter removes most nodes, so the graph walk can hit dead ends where no matching neighbour is linked. Engines add filter-aware links when payload indexes exist before indexing, explore two hops (Weaviate's ACORN), keep scanning until enough rows pass (pgvector iterative scans), or switch to an exact scan of the matching ids when the set is small.

mistakes.mistake: Taking the top 10 and filtering in application code
mistakes.fix: Pass the filter into the vector query, or oversample by about 10 ÷ selectivity

mistakes.mistake: Filtering on fields with no index or with inconsistent values
mistakes.fix: Index every filtered field and normalise values such as “MH” and “Maharashtra” at ingestion

quiz.question: An insurer’s search takes the ANN top 10 and then keeps only motor circulars for Maharashtra, which are 0.5% of chunks. On average, how many results survive?
quiz.explanation: Expected survivors = k × selectivity = 10 × 0.005 = 0.05, so the list is usually empty.

quiz.question: A marketplace post-filters by “in stock in Pune”, which matches 4% of products. How many candidates must the ANN search fetch so that about 10 survive on average?
quiz.explanation: 10 ÷ 0.04 = 250 candidates. The rarer the filter, the more oversampling post-filtering needs.

quiz.question: A bank’s RBI circular search filters on department = “Payments”, which matches 30% of 5 lakh chunks. Which strategy is usually the poorest fit?
options: Filtered ANN with a payload index
Pre-filtering with an exact scan of every matching chunk
quiz.explanation: 30% of 5 lakh is 1,50,000 vectors to score exactly on every query. Broad filters suit filtered ANN or modest oversampling.

quiz.question: A filter matches 8,000 of 20 lakh chunks. Qdrant has a payload index on every filtered field. What is its planner likely to do?
options: Walk the HNSW graph and hope enough nodes match
Read the matching ids from the payload index and score them exactly
Return an error for low cardinality
quiz.explanation: For a small matching set, an exact scan is cheap and gives 100% recall; the payload index supplies the cardinality estimate.

quiz.question: A UPI dispute knowledge base stores the state as “MH” on some chunks and “Maharashtra” on others. Queries filter on “MH”. What happens?
options: Both match, because they mean the same thing
The query fails with an error
quiz.explanation: Filters are exact conditions. Normalise metadata values at ingestion.

quiz.question: A hospital’s guideline search should use only the current version of each protocol. What is the most reliable way?
options: Add “use the latest version” to the prompt
Store version or is_current as metadata and filter on it in the vector query
Embed the version number into the text
quiz.explanation: A structured filter guarantees the condition; prompt text and embeddings only encourage it.

quiz.question: Which are good candidates for metadata filters in a policy-wording search? Select all that apply.
options: Product line, such as motor or health
quiz.explanation: Filters work on hard, structured facts. Tone is fuzzy and belongs to ranking, not filtering.

quiz.question: With pgvector 0.8, a filtered HNSW query returns only 3 rows for LIMIT 10. Which setting keeps scanning the index until enough rows pass the WHERE clause?
quiz.explanation: Iterative index scans (strict_order or relaxed_order) continue the scan until enough filtered rows are found, up to max_scan_tuples.

quiz.question: Why should Qdrant payload indexes be created before a large bulk upload rather than after?
options: The HNSW graph can then be built with extra links that keep filtered searches connected
quiz.explanation: Qdrant builds filter-aware links when payload indexes exist at indexing time; adding them later misses that benefit until reindexing.

quiz.question: A SEBI-circular assistant embeds the query “circulars from 2025 on margin”. Results include 2019 circulars. What is missing?
options: A structured date filter instead of relying on the words “from 2025”
quiz.explanation: Embeddings blur dates. A range filter on the issue date enforces it.

quiz.question: Which signs suggest post-filtering is hurting recall? Select all that apply.
options: Rare filters return fewer than k results
Recall is fine on unfiltered queries but poor on filtered ones
Latency rises steadily with collection size for all queries
Raising the candidate count fills the empty slots
quiz.explanation: Short lists on rare filters, a gap between filtered and unfiltered recall, and relief from oversampling all point to post-filtering.

quiz.question: Suraksha General pre-filters exactly. Scoring costs about 0.1 ms per 1,000 vectors. A filter matches 50% of 20 lakh chunks. About how long does the scan take?
quiz.explanation: 10,00,000 vectors × 0.1 ms per 1,000 = 100 ms. Broad filters make exact pre-filtering slow.

quiz.question: A citizen-services search must show only schemes for the user’s state and must never mix in other departments’ internal notes. Which part belongs to metadata filtering, and which to a separate control?
options: State is a relevance filter; blocking internal notes is access control and needs its own enforcement
State needs access control; internal notes need a re-ranker
quiz.explanation: Relevance filters narrow results; permissions and tenancy are a security boundary with their own design and tests.

quiz.question: A Weaviate collection has a very restrictive filter and filtered HNSW recall drops. Which strategy targets this case?
options: ACORN, which explores two-hop neighbours when direct ones are filtered out
quiz.explanation: ACORN keeps the graph walk connected when most neighbours fail the filter.

quiz.question: A search filters on merchant_category with 12 possible values but has no index on that field. What is the likely effect?
options: Each query checks the field on far more records than needed, adding latency and hurting planning
quiz.explanation: Unindexed filter fields force slow checks and prevent the engine from estimating cardinality.

quiz.question: A clinical-note search post-filters by ward. Which fixes restore a full top 10 for rare wards? Select all that apply.
options: Pass the filter into the vector query
Pre-filter and score the matching notes exactly when there are few
quiz.explanation: Filter inside the search, oversample enough, or scan the small matching set exactly. A smaller k just hides the problem.

quiz.question: An NBFC filters loan-policy chunks by product and version. Recall is 98% on broad filters and 40% on rare ones. What should the evaluation report?
options: Recall and latency per selectivity band: broad, medium and rare
quiz.explanation: Filter strategies fail differently by selectivity, so an average hides the rare-filter collapse.

quiz.question: A filter matches 5% of chunks. Post-filtering fetches 40 candidates. How many results survive on average?
quiz.explanation: 40 × 0.05 = 2 of the 10 slots filled.

quiz.question: Which statement about Pinecone metadata filters is accurate?
options: They are applied during the vector query, so results match the filter
They are applied only after results reach your application
They work only on vector values
They require a separate SQL database
quiz.explanation: Pinecone applies metadata filters inside the query using operators such as $eq, $in and $gte.

quiz.question: A bank moves from post-filtering to filtered ANN with payload indexes. What else should the team do? Select all that apply.
options: Remove the date field to save memory
Check that every filtered field has an index
quiz.explanation: Clean values, indexed fields and per-band measurement make filtered search trustworthy.
